A resurgence of another monsoon surge, induced by various fast-
developing systems embedded within the vast monsoon trough to the
north, is expected to bring increasing winds, showers and 
thunderstorms to the region. At this time, the surge south of a 
regenerated Tropical Depression Kujira (14W) is expected to trip over
Tinian and Saipan, with 20-25 mph southwesterlies occasionally 
gusting to 35 mph near potentially heavy showers Monday. The leading 
edge of these surges are expected to anchor themselves over Tinian 
and Saipan through midweek, as a secondary disturbance follows an 
eastward- propagating Kujira and induces a much more persistent surge
thereafter. This will allow convection to then shift southward, 
spreading on-and-off showers and thunderstorms across the rest of the
CNMI and Guam. However, these conditions are not expected to be 
conducive for flash flooding, so a Flood Watch is not yet warranted 
but may be considered for Tinian and Saipan the next day or so. 
Conditions are expected to improve considerably in the second half of
the week once these systems move away from the area and a tropical 
ridge forms in western Micronesia, introducing drier diffusive flow 
across the Marianas for the rest of the week.

Marine...
Combined seas of 8 to 11 feet are expected over the next few days,
remaining hazardous to small craft through at least early Tuesday
morning. Seas look to fall below hazardous levels for Guam and 
Rota by midweek, but are expected to remain hazardous for Tinian 
and Saipan into the latter half of the week as the southern edge 
of the monsoon surge persists over the area. 

Tropical Systems...
The remnants of Tropical Depression 13W have strengthened, and we now
have TD Kujira again (13W) located west of the Maug Islands near
21.9N 142.23E. Kujira is forecast to turn east, increase its forward
speed, and become a tropical storm once again by Monday afternoon.

Next on the list is Invest 98W, currently 300 miles east-
northeast of the Maug Islands, as it's currently near 20N153E. 
This disturbance is rated as "Medium" by JTWC, meaning development
of a tropical cyclone is likely beyond 24 hours. Conditions are 
favorable for both the TCFA and 98W to continue to organize, and 
the models also show this will occur with 98W as it also heads for
an area north of Wake Island during the next few days.

Then we have another circulation, dubbed invest 99W, which is 
located near along the monsoon trough near 22N166E. This 
disturbance lacks a true LLCC per scatterometer analysis and 
visible imagery loops. This looks to be more an artifact of a 
monsoon vortex co-located at the end of a monsoon trough and 
within a favorable environment, with no development expected. 
Still, given sharp bending in the streamline analysis and some 
localized elevated convection, the "Sub-Low" rating from JTWC is 
warranted, and we'll keep an eye on it.

Finally, we have an area of cyclonic rotation that we've been
watching for a few days now, northeast of Majuro near 10N173E. The
cyclonic low-level flow around the LLCC has strengthened markedly
since yesterday, as evident in the visible loop imagery. This 
circulation is at the tail end monsoon trough. The increased 
cyclonic flow has allowed for convection to increase from near 
Kosrae to Majuro, as westerly flow south of the LLCC has 
strengthened. With that said, we still expect this system to head
west to the RMI chain with a steady state in development, before 
possibly drifting west-southwest to east of Pohnpei/north of 
Kosrae while it weakens, with this expected to occur over the next
48 to 72 hours. With that said, JTWC and WFO Guam continue to 
watch this feature for possible Invest inclusion.

For more information please refer to bulletins from the Joint
Typhoon Warning Center under WMO header ABPW10 PGTW.

Eastern Micronesia...
Showers have developed across between Pohnpei and the RMI chair to
include Kosrae, where a few showers in that vicinity are of moderate
intensity, as evident by -60 deg. C cloud top temperatures. 
Otherwise, any rainfall has been lift, with the moisture surge (that 
we talked about the past couple of days), as evident by PWATs 
(Precipitable Water Values near or above 2.5 inches area-wide. 
However, divergence is weak, allowing for mainly mid to high level 
cloud cover and light showers to persist. Perhaps, we'll see another
nocturnal (nighttime) flare-up later tonight. Still, given how mist 
the atmosphere has become, carried scattered to numerous showers at 
Kosrae, and scattered showers elsewhere. Additional disturbances look
to keep the weather unsettled over the next several days, as they 
cross the Date Line and head west.

Western Micronesia...
Satellite imagery shows mostly clear to partly cloudy skies across
western Micronesia. Altimetry shows combined seas of 4 to 7 feet
across the region.
